subject: Physics
title: Work, Energy and Power
summary: Work is done when there is displacement along the force: W = F·s = Fs cos θ. A force perpendicular to motion (centripetal force, normal force) does zero work. Work can also be negative (friction).
The work–energy theorem is the biggest shortcut: work done by ALL forces = change in KE. It gives speeds without worrying about how forces vary with time.

The work of a conservative force (gravity, spring, electric) is path-independent, and a potential energy U is defined for it: F = −dU/dx. If only conservative forces do work, mechanical energy (KE + PE) stays constant. Friction is non-conservative — energy becomes heat.

Power = rate of doing work, P = dW/dt = F·v. In collisions momentum is always conserved (with no external force), but KE only in elastic collisions; the coefficient of restitution e tells how elastic the collision was.

formulas.name: Work by a constant force
formulas.formula: W = F·s = Fs cos θ = F_x s_x + F_y s_y + F_z s_z
formulas.mistake: θ is between force and DISPLACEMENT, not between force and the surface.

formulas.name: Work by a variable force
formulas.formula: W = ∫F dx = area under the F–x graph
formulas.when: Force varying with position (spring, F = kx²).
formulas.note: Area below the x-axis is negative work.

formulas.name: Kinetic energy
formulas.mistake: For equal momentum the lighter body has more KE — not the other way round.

formulas.name: Work–energy theorem
formulas.when: Speed with friction, air resistance or variable forces.
formulas.mistake: Add the work of ALL forces (gravity, friction, normal, applied), not just one.

formulas.name: Gravitational potential energy (near earth)
formulas.formula: U = mgh  (h from a reference level)
formulas.note: Any reference level gives the same ΔU — absolute U has no meaning.

formulas.name: Spring potential energy
formulas.formula: F = −kx;   U = ½kx²;   work by spring from x₁ to x₂ = ½k(x₁² − x₂²)
formulas.mistake: Measure x from the natural length, not the total length.

formulas.name: Force from potential energy
formulas.formula: F = −dU/dx;   equilibrium: dU/dx = 0;   stable: d²U/dx² > 0, unstable: < 0
formulas.when: When U(x) is given as a graph or function.
formulas.mistake: Don't forget the minus sign: force acts towards decreasing U.

formulas.name: Conservation of mechanical energy
formulas.formula: K_i + U_i = K_f + U_f  (only conservative forces doing work)
formulas.note: With friction it doesn't apply directly — add W_friction.

formulas.name: Power
formulas.formula: P_avg = W/t;   P = dW/dt = F·v = Fv cos θ;   1 hp = 746 W
formulas.mistake: kWh is a unit of energy, not power (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J).

formulas.name: Vertical circle (string)
formulas.formula: Minimum speed at bottom √(5gl);  at top √(gl);  T_bottom − T_top = 6mg
formulas.when: Ball on a string completing the circle.
formulas.mistake: For a rod (not a string) the minimum is 0 at the top and √(4gl) at the bottom.

formulas.name: Elastic collision in 1-D
formulas.formula: v₁ = [(m₁ − m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁ + m₂);   v₂ = [(m₂ − m₁)u₂ + 2m₁u₁]/(m₁ + m₂)
formulas.note: Equal masses simply exchange velocities — no formula needed.

formulas.name: Perfectly inelastic collision
formulas.formula: v = (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂)/(m₁ + m₂);   KE loss = m₁m₂(u₁ − u₂)² / [2(m₁ + m₂)]
formulas.mistake: Assuming KE is conserved is wrong — only momentum is.

formulas.name: Coefficient of restitution
formulas.formula: e = (speed of separation)/(speed of approach) = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂);   e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic
formulas.note: Be careful with signs — take both approach and separation as positive.

formulas.name: Bouncing ball
formulas.formula: Rebound height h₁ = e²h;   nth rebound hₙ = e²ⁿh
formulas.mistake: Speed is multiplied by e, height by e² — don't mix them.

formulas.name: Collision in 2-D
formulas.formula: Separately in each direction: Σp_x conserved, Σp_y conserved.  Equal masses, elastic, one at rest ⇒ they move off at 90°
formulas.mistake: Adding speeds directly is wrong — add vectors (components).

examples.title: Work from a dot product
examples.problem: F = (3î + 4ĵ) N, displacement s = (2î + ĵ) m. Work?

examples.title: Variable force
examples.problem: F = 3x² N (x in metres). Work from x = 0 to 2 m?

examples.title: Block from a spring
examples.problem: A spring with k = 200 N/m is compressed 0.1 m and releases a 0.5 kg block (smooth floor). Spring energy and block speed?

examples.title: Power of a motor
examples.problem: A motor lifts 100 kg at a constant 2 m/s (g = 10). Power?
examples.solution: Constant speed ⇒ F = mg = 1000 N. P = Fv = 1000 × 2 = 2000 W (≈ 2.7 hp).

examples.title: Vertical circle
examples.problem: A 0.5 kg ball on a 1 m string must complete a vertical circle (g = 10). Minimum speeds at bottom and top, and the difference in tension?
examples.solution: Bottom: √(5gl) = √50 ≈ 7.07 m/s. Top: √(gl) = √10 ≈ 3.16 m/s. T_bottom − T_top = 6mg = 30 N.

examples.title: Elastic collision
examples.problem: A 2 kg block at 3 m/s collides elastically with a 1 kg block at rest. Final velocities?

examples.title: Sticking collision
examples.problem: A 2 kg block at 3 m/s hits a 1 kg block at rest and they stick. Common velocity and KE loss?
examples.solution: v = 6/3 = 2 m/s. KE before 9 J, after ½ × 3 × 4 = 6 J ⇒ loss = 3 J (heat/sound).

examples.title: Bouncing ball
examples.problem: A ball is dropped from 5 m with e = 0.6. First rebound height?

examples.title: Stopping by friction
examples.problem: A 2 kg block slides at 10 m/s on a rough floor (μ_k = 0.25). How far before it stops?
examples.solution: Work–energy: μmg·s = ½mv² ⇒ s = v²/(2μg) = 100/5 = 20 m. (Mass cancels.)

examples.title: 2-D sticking collision
examples.problem: A 2 kg body moving east at 3 m/s and a 3 kg body moving north at 2 m/s collide and stick. Final velocity?
examples.solution: p_x = 6, p_y = 6 kg·m/s ⇒ v = √(36 + 36)/5 ≈ 1.7 m/s, at 45° north of east.

examples.title: Work done by air resistance
examples.problem: A 2 kg stone falls 5 m and hits the ground at 8 m/s (g = 10). Work done by air resistance?
examples.solution: W_gravity = mgh = 100 J. ΔK = ½ × 2 × 64 = 64 J. W_air = 64 − 100 = −36 J (negative — energy taken away).

topics.title: When work is zero, positive or negative
topics.explain: θ < 90° positive (force helps motion); θ = 90° zero (normal force, centripetal force, gravity on a porter walking horizontally with a load); θ > 90° negative (friction, gravity on a ball thrown up).

topics.title: Kinetic and potential energy
topics.explain: KE is energy of motion, always ≥ 0. PE is energy of position/configuration (height, stretch of a spring) — defined only for conservative forces. Unit joule; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

topics.title: Work–energy theorem
topics.explain: Net work = ΔKE. It is the integral form of Newton's second law and the fastest way to get speed with variable forces, curved paths or friction.

topics.title: Conservative vs non-conservative forces
topics.explain: Conservative: work is path-independent, zero over a closed loop, and PE is defined (gravity, spring, electrostatic). Non-conservative: work depends on path and energy becomes heat (friction, air drag, viscous force).

topics.title: Potential energy of a spring
topics.explain: Stretching a spring by x needs work ½kx², stored as PE. The spring force is restoring (F = −kx). Two springs: in series 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, in parallel k = k₁ + k₂.

topics.title: Motion in a vertical circle
topics.explain: Speed falls going up (KE → PE). For the string not to slacken, T ≥ 0 at the top ⇒ v_top ≥ √(gl), and energy gives v_bottom ≥ √(5gl). At the horizontal position tension = mv²/l.

topics.title: Collisions: elastic and inelastic
topics.explain: In every collision (no external force) momentum is conserved. In elastic collisions KE is also conserved (e = 1) — atomic or ideal billiard collisions. In inelastic ones some KE becomes heat/sound/deformation. In perfectly inelastic collisions the bodies stick and KE loss is maximum.

topics.title: Collisions in two dimensions
topics.explain: Conserve x and y momentum separately. In an elastic oblique collision of equal masses (one at rest) they move off at 90° (billiards). In head-on (1-D) collisions everything is along one line.

ratta: W = Fs cos θ;  W_net = ΔK.
Perfectly inelastic: maximum KE loss, e = 0.
